quote: It says this year as of March 2026, my kilowatt hours is two eighty seven. And last year, it was one ninety five.
stewart_read: The customer hands over a striking data point — usage up 47% year over year — entirely unprompted, and the rep's only response is a flat acknowledgment before moving to the next data point. This was the single clearest bill-anchor opportunity on the call and it was filed, not flipped.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged that flipping mid-bill-collection would derail the data-gathering flow and planned to let the closer use the number instead — but there is no evidence in the transcript of the rep flagging this for the closer or returning to it later, so the reactive read holds.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to reflect big usage swings back to the customer in the moment ('that jump is exactly the kind of thing solar locks in against') rather than only logging the number for the design.

quote: Yes. My mother is on the title with me. Her name is Gail Braemer.
stewart_read: A co-owner was identified by name, which is the same structural trigger as the spouse_decision protocol — the person on title should be included in the appointment. The rep never revisits whether Gail should be on the closer call.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged the mother's involvement was covered implicitly by the credit-qualifier question about her ('do you know if that'd be the case for you or your mother') — but that question is about credit, not appointment attendance, so it does not substitute for inviting her.
coaching_implication: Any co-owner named on title should trigger an explicit ask — 'let's get your mom on the call too since she's on the title' — before booking. This appointment is now vulnerable to a decision-maker being absent, the same risk flagged in protocols.spouse_decision.

quote: I think the city of Denver offers some financial assistance to get solar panels, so I'm considering that as well.
stewart_read: Customer discloses they are actively weighing a municipal assistance program as an alternative path — competitive context the closer would benefit from knowing. The rep does not probe (what program, has she applied, timeline) and moves straight into the address confirmation.
alternative_hypothesis: This may not be a true competitive threat since city assistance programs and private solar installs aren't mutually exclusive, so probing may have been low-value — but the rep doesn't even note it for the handoff, which is the lower-cost miss regardless of threat level.
coaching_implication: When a customer mentions a parallel program or alternative path, even briefly, a 10-second probe ('have you looked into that yet, or still just considering it?') gives the closer useful framing without costing call time.

quote: if I did qualify and I get solar panels and there's a certain number, right, that you put on the house, like, would I need to get more added if I get a charger added?
stewart_read: Customer owns an EV bought in September and is actively planning a future charger/garage addition — a concrete future-load signal that increases the value of a rightsized or expandable system. The rep handled the redirect correctly by deferring to the specialist, but did not reflect the signal back as a reason to get excited about the appointment.
coaching_implication: This is a case where the scope-hold was correct, but the rep could have paired it with an anchor line ('good news is the specialist can design around that future load') to build appointment anticipation instead of just closing the topic.

quote: That's a really good question. I would bring that up to a specialist.
stewart_read: This is actually the correct move, not scope creep — flagged here to note it as a positive example: the rep resisted answering a technical panel-sizing question and bridged cleanly to the specialist using the universal escape hatch pattern.
coaching_implication: Use this as the positive model when coaching other reps on EV/expansion questions — bridge, don't explain.

quote: one of the reasons why I wanna save on electricity is the financial strain is difficult.
stewart_read: Customer discloses financial strain in the same breath as being unsure of their credit score — a vulnerability disclosure per schema. The rep's response is a bare acknowledgment ('I gotcha. But No problem.') before continuing the credit-score line of questioning.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have intentionally kept the moment brief to avoid dwelling on a sensitive topic mid-qualification — but the schema treats this disclosure as a trust gift warranting at least a specific acknowledgment before moving on, which didn't happen here.
coaching_implication: A one-line specific acknowledgment ('that's exactly the kind of thing this program is built to help with') before returning to the credit question would validate the disclosure without derailing the flow.
